newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Moscow discards NATO megaphone in Eastern Europe.
newsitem.headline: Moscow discards NATO megaphone in Eastern Europe.

text.p: Unlike in its dealings with the West, Russia is treading softly in eastern European capitals as it campaigns to block NATO's expansion. But quiet diplomacy has produced few results, except perhaps in Slovakia and Bulgaria.
NATO expansion now seems unstoppable, with U.S. President Bill Clinton calling this week for the first former East Bloc states to join the Western alliance by 1999.

In the East, most nations are determined to leave the security vacuum they have lived in since the fall of communism. Their governments, including those led by ex-communists, firmly but politely resist any Russian veto over their ambitions.
Diplomats say Moscow has largely respected this determination, nothwithstanding occasional lapses, saving its threats of dire consequences for a Western audience.
But where governments are perceived, rightly or wrongly, to be wavering, Moscow has been quick to mount charm offensives.
Russia has long used megaphone diplomacy to oppose NATO plans to recruit countries which were its allies until 1989.
President Boris Yeltsin has warned that NATO expansion would fan the flame of war across Europe. But Moscow is taking a softly-softly approach with the NATO aspirants themselves.
"There hasn't been too much direct pressure on us," said one senior Czech diplomat. "We are not their primary target."
In Prague, the political establishment from President Vaclav Havel down is united in seeking NATO membership, although polls show ordinary Czechs to be more sceptical.
Most countries run by former communists, notably Poland, Hungary and Romania -- which took an independent line even when it was in the Warsaw Pact -- are equally determined.

But Hungary witnessed one of Moscow's occasional lapses earlier this year. "Should Hungary join NATO, Russia would be forced to take countermeasures. As NATO is a military organisation, Russia would also take measures of a military nature," Russian ambassador Ivan Aboimov was quoted as saying.
The Hungarian foreign ministry expressed surprise at Aboimov's remarks but the controversy soon fizzled out.
Unlike other eastern Europeans, Bulgarians traditionally regard Russians as liberators rather than dominators and the Socialist government shows little enthusiasm for joining NATO.

Ivan Marazov, Socialist candidate in presidential elections, has proposed a referendum. "The Bulgarian people are still not aware of the advantages of NATO membership. They are not sure whether NATO would guarantee security," he said.
Things are a little less clear in Slovakia, a former frontunner for early NATO membership which has slipped due to a turbulent political scene in the past two years.
New Foreign Minister Pavol Hamzik has mounted an energetic campaign to get Bratislava back among the vanguard when NATO makes its decision early next year on whom to recruit.
But the Slovak leadership has sometimes sent contradictory signals. In May Jan Luptak, who leads a far-left party in the coalition, said Slovakia was striving for neutrality.
The foreign ministry quickly dismissed this comment but the opposition has accused Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar of trying to revive old friendships to the east.
Meciar has stressed Slovakia's commitment to joining NATO if voters approve membership in a referendum.
But he has said it is important to understand Russia's economic influence and stressed the need to appreciate "all parties" in creating a new central European security structure.
In words reminiscent of Yeltsin's, he said: "Otherwise there is a danger of a new polarisation in Europe..."
Moscow has responded generously, offering a free-trade zone to help offset a big Slovak trade deficit with Russia.
But Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov also had some advice when he visited Bratislava in February. "It is in our interest that your goods are exported to Russia," he said.
"Do not get too involved with NATO," he added. "NATO comes and goes. Nations remain."
